subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage: Monday. In the school corridor, some classmates laughed at Noor's faded uniform and said, "Her mother stitches for our mothers." Noor kept walking, jaw tight, and ate lunch in the library. Wednesday. Noor finally told Anirban, the class teacher, what had been happening for weeks. Anirban put down his pen. "Thank you for telling me. That's not right, and it's not your fault. I believe you." Anirban asked what would help, and Noor said, "Please don't make it a big scene." Friday. In class Anirban spoke about respect for every kind of work and every family, without naming anyone. At lunch a classmate, Neha, dropped her bag beside Noor. "Can I sit here?" Noor nodded, surprised by the lightness in her chest.

qa.q: Where did Noor eat lunch on Monday?
qa.a: Noor ate lunch in the library on Monday.

qa.q: How did Noor feel while walking away on Monday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Noor felt hurt and humiliated. Noor's jaw was tight and lunch was eaten in the library to avoid the classmates.

qa.q: What turning point on Wednesday changed things?
qa.a: Noor told Anirban what had been happening, and Anirban said it was not Noor's fault and believed Noor, which led to the class talk on Friday.

qa.q: How might Neha have seen Noor when asking to sit down?
qa.a: Neha may have noticed Noor eating alone and wanted to include Noor. Asking permission shows respect rather than pity.

grounding: A teenager is mocked for a faded uniform and family work, then is believed and supported by a teacher and a classmate.

subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage: Leela, you asked why I always keep one extra chair at my table. Sit, I'll tell you. I am Ira, and at fifteen I was invited to Sunita's birthday. When I arrived, Sunita's aunt looked at my surname on the gift tag and said, "The seats are all taken." Everyone else was sitting. I stood holding the parcel while my face burned. Then our teacher Mr. Verma, who was a guest, said, "Then let us bring another chair," and carried one over himself. On Monday he asked me quietly whether I was all right and said, "I saw it. It was wrong, and you did nothing to deserve it." I still remember that chair. The next week Sunita came to my house with her mother, who apologised. So now I keep a chair.

qa.q: What did Sunita's aunt say when Ira arrived?
qa.a: Sunita's aunt looked at the surname on the gift tag and said, "The seats are all taken."

qa.q: How did young Ira feel standing with the parcel?
qa.a: Ira felt humiliated and hurt. Ira's face burned as everyone else sat while Ira stood.

qa.q: What choice did Mr. Verma make at the party that changed the moment?
qa.a: He said they would bring another chair and carried one over himself, treating the problem as easy to solve and not making Ira feel like a burden.

qa.q: How might Sunita's mother have felt when she came to apologise?
qa.a: Probably ashamed of what happened and wanting to make it right. Coming to the house shows she took it seriously.

grounding: A teenager is denied a seat because of a surname, and a teacher and later a host family recognise it as wrong and support the wounded teenager.
